pr_title: run: add option to prevent the setting of terminal title
pr_body:
There is an environment variable (and a CLI option) to turn off color tinting, so there should equally be a way to turn off title setting, as both are pretty much parts of the same feature.

Closes https://github.com/systemd/systemd/issues/33301
pr_comments: Please just make this an envvar. There's no need to add a whole new option for turning off such cosmetic stuff.
yeah there's already an env var for background tinting, this sounds like should be handled in the same way, an env var should be enough

Note that the --background option allows one to customize the background color, so that more or less makes sense. But here the option is only to disable the setting of title, which is not very useful.

> yeah there's already an env var for background tinting, this sounds like should be handled in the same way, an env var should be enough

Is that env var documented anywhere?

> > yeah there's already an env var for background tinting, this sounds like should be handled in the same way, an env var should be enough
> 
> Is that env var documented anywhere?

SYSTEMD_TINT_BACKGROUND in docs/ENVIRONMENT.md

> > > yeah there's already an env var for background tinting, this sounds like should be handled in the same way, an env var should be enough
> > 
> > 
> > Is that env var documented anywhere?
> 
> SYSTEMD_TINT_BACKGROUND in docs/ENVIRONMENT.md

Which is nowhere near `man systemd-run` when I looked, so it might as well not exist as far as I know. I had tried grepping for `getenv`, but I really no longer have enough energy to chase through source code for things like that...

I replaced the option with an envvar, and attempted to document both in the manpage, but it's my first attempt at writing docbook in any way, so I haven't yet figured out how to add a reference link to the full ENVIRONMENT doc.
Please squash the commit introducing SYSTEMD_RUN_SET_TITLE into the one that made the envvar generic.

hmm, i am ok with allowing this to be turned off, but i wonder what you actually want to turn off here, because if you don#t want apps to change your terminal title, then maybe tell your terminal emulator that rather turning it off in each app.

Hence, I guess what you actually don#t like is the colored dot prefix? did i get this right? then maybe make that something you can disable, not the general title setting (who knows what we might use it for).

I mean, let's just take a step back, and figure out what is actually the goal here.

i read the original issue, which left me more confused, i.e. it seems there are multiple things that aren't liked, but the ability to just turn off everything seems the least ideal way to address this. i mean i don't like options. I'd much rather find a way that just works out of the box for everyone. I initially though the issue was the colorful dot, but i think the issue is now about the length of the title on long command lines. The answer to that I am sure is that we should ellipsize though.

> i read the original issue, which left me more confused, i.e. it seems there are multiple things that aren't liked, but the ability to just turn off everything seems the least ideal way to address this. i mean i don't like options. I'd much rather find a way that just works out of the box for everyone. I initially though the issue was the colorful dot, but i think the issue is now about the length of the title on long command lines. The answer to that I am sure is that we should ellipsize though. 

We had a discussion on Mastodon: https://social.treehouse.systems/@grawity/112631942075330469

Basically @grawity wants to keep the title set by the actual service process. And I think that's a valid request, especially for systemd-run. That information, if provided, is almost certainly more meaningful than the plain cmdline passed.

> hmm, i am ok with allowing this to be turned off, but i wonder what you actually want to turn off here, because if you don#t want apps to change your terminal title, then maybe tell your terminal emulator that rather turning it off in each app.

No, that's not what I said. I don't want to turn off titles in general – on the contrary, I already have programs set up to set a more useful title than systemd-run does, so I want to disable this in systemd-run specifically.

I mean, the new `run0` is an app that gets to set its own title in whatever way it wants, but systemd-run was never that – it's something that so far has been advertised as being a scriptable tool and so on, and I've been using it as part of scripts and tools and other things. (For example, in a backup script that sets a window title according to what it's backing up, and then calls something through systemd-run or directly depending on situation. It doesn't run an interactive shell, so the privilege indication is unneeded, too.)

So the primary goal is to preserve whatever title has been set, either by the shell or by a wrapper script. (The secondary goal is to remove the red dot for aesthetics.)

> I initially though the issue was the colorful dot, but i think the issue is now about the length of the title on long command lines

I re-thought this... but it really is about all of it. Not necessarily for the same reason, but the sum is that I'd still like to turn off the _entire_ feature, and not just to fix any specific part of it.

> I'd much rather find a way that just works out of the box for everyone

Well, you already have that: there are two separate tools now, which wrap the same functionality for different use cases that have different needs. I thought the entire point of introducing run0 was that it could have different behavior from systemd-run, wasn't it?

(I was actually planning to make a second PR that would keep this default-on in run0, but make it default-off in systemd-run.)

Making this tied to `--shell` would make sense, since mostly it's just interactive shells that can really make use of the "elevated window" indication (and they typically set their own titles anyway, so it doesn't matter if the old title was overwritten). But I doubt it can be reliably detected depending on what's being run, or anything like that.

Well, the moment use --pty you are invoking systemd-run as an interactive tool with ansi sequence terminal mgmt stuff and so on, I think setting the title when we take over your terminal to that level I think might actually be ok. 

Why do you specify "--pty" in your case btw? why not just invoke that tool without?

> Well, the moment use --pty you are invoking systemd-run as an interactive tool with ansi sequence terminal mgmt stuff and so on, I think setting the title when we take over your terminal to that level I think might actually be ok.

No, I didn't sign up for this "ansi sequence terminal mgmt stuff" in the first place; that's not what --pty was documented as doing. It's circular justification.

> Why do you specify "--pty" in your case btw? why not just invoke that tool without?

In this case – it shows progress information, which doesn't work nearly as well when it goes over a pipe.

issue_context.title: RFE: Environment variable to stop systemd-run from setting a window title
issue_context.body:
### Component

systemd-run

### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe

When `systemd-run --pty` is active, it overwrites the previously-set terminal title with a copy of the command being run (plus a colourful dot for whatever reason). This is 1) hideous but also 2) makes the title actually useless in situations when something else than an interactive shell is run – my backup tool uses `systemd-run --pty borg` as part of the process, so while it would previously show what job was being run, now it only shows a mile-long borg command line.

### Describe the solution you'd like

Would like either a systemd-run option or an environment variable to disable both the background-setting and the title-setting.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

I was considering switching my backup tool back to using `sudo` or `doas` (as it already had the fallback code from back when systemd-run was still new).

### The systemd version you checked that didn't have the feature you are asking for

256
comments:
> (plus a colourful dot for whatever reason). This is 1) hideous but also 2) makes the title actually useless in situations when something else than an interactive shell is run – my backup tool uses `systemd-run --pty borg` as part of the process, so while it would previously show what job was being run, now it only shows a mile-long borg command line.

i don't grok this? what did it previously show precisely? what does "previously showed job" mean? what is "job"?

if the cmdline is too long for display and the WM doesn't sensible shorten it, we maybe should just ellipsize it ourselves, we have easy calls for that.

the colorful dot tells you about raised privs: if it's red. Or if you enetered a container or a VM.

anyway, please explain more precisely what the problem is, i.e.:

1. you don't like the dot?
2. we don't ellipsize the title?
3. …?

To rephrase OP's issue:

Lots of things set the terminal title, but `systemd-run` (or `run0`) will ask the terminal to change the title and the terminal will happily do that. So if you've configured your terminal to have an informational title of some kind, `systemd-run` will trample all over that.

In this case, it sounds like the user has some sort of orchestration infrastructure that sets the terminal title to something meaningful and then runs some tool with privileges. For example, maybe they have a script that looks something like this:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/bash

[...]

for location in /path/a /path/b /path/c /path/d; do
   set_terminal_title "Backup: $location"
   systemd-run --pty borg --lots --of --args $location
done
```

The script should change the terminal title to indicate the status of the script. So let's say the title should say "Backup: /path/c". Instead, it will say "🔴 borg --lots --of --args /path/c", which makes the output a lot less useful

> if the cmdline is too long for display and the WM doesn't sensible shorten it, we maybe should just ellipsize it ourselves, we have easy calls for that.

IMO, strong NACK. Truncating the title of the tab belongs to the UI, not to command line tools. The UI knows how much text will fit in the tab title, `systemd-run` does not.

> the colorful dot tells you about raised privs: if it's red. Or if you enetered a container or a VM.

IMO, I'm not the biggest fan of this (and the background changing) either.

The background changing can be just straight-up buggy when faced with ncurses applications, especially if those applications crash. Terminal emulators can't handle full-screen background color changes very well whenever they have to scroll, or resize:

![Screenshot from 2024-06-18 17-02-31](https://github.com/systemd/systemd/assets/11251606/aed426cd-2e13-42b0-a0ca-912136bb960f)

It is also entirely unaware of the color scheme of the terminal, and so it has the nice side-effect of making text in the terminal hard-to-read due to lack of contrast.

Essentially, this should really be the job of the terminal emulator, at least for interactive tasks. Modern GNOME terminal emulators will indicate when you're running something as root, or in a container, by recoloring the appropriate parts of a window red / purple / whatever, and changing the terminal color scheme appropriately. For instance:

![Screenshot from 2024-06-18 17-08-48](https://github.com/systemd/systemd/assets/11251606/50832c49-873e-4176-9d0c-09d1ccca92c9)

The red dot is entirely redundant here, and actually counter-productive in some cases because this specific terminal emulator will actually show the icon of the container manager if it detects that you're inside of a container.

I understand it's for situations like the VT where there's no terminal emulator to save you. Maybe we should just detect `TERM=Linux` and turn it on then. Maybe we turn off the recoloring when you're in an interactive terminal? IDK the solution here but this pretty printing logic makes it feel buggy...

Still not daily driving this on Fedora w/ v256 (Don't have v256 yet), so maybe this was all fixed between my last build of it & release. But I suspect not, most of these bugs are caused by the terminal emulator.

> the colorful dot tells you about raised privs: if it's red. Or if you enetered a container or a VM.

Just my 2 cents: The red dot emoji reminds me of a record button (conditioned by usage in camera apps), so when i see this icon, i expect it is indicating that the screen is recorded.

Maybe there is a better way to indicate raised privileges, but i doubt i can be done with an emoji. I can't think of a fitting emoji for this use case.

> IMO, strong NACK. Truncating the title of the tab belongs to the UI, not to command line tools. The UI knows how much text will fit in the tab title, `systemd-run` does not.

Well, not sure I agree. Right now we'd happily send a 1MB title to the terminal, which doesn't really make much sense. We should ellipsize overly long stuff. What's up for discussion though is just where to place the cutoff, i.e. already after 100ch or so, or more at 16K or so?

> Terminal emulators can't handle full-screen background color changes very well whenever they have to scroll, or resize:

Yeah, they really should take the bg color of the last character of a visible line into account when rebreaking things and inserting new whitespace.

> It is also entirely unaware of the color scheme of the terminal, and so it has the nice side-effect of making text in the terminal hard-to-read due to lack of contrast.

That's not actually true. We read the bg color from the terminal, and then shift it into a red hue. Maybe the algorithm for shifting the hue could be tweaked, but it's not true that we are "entirely unaware" of the color scheme. We are very much aware.

> Essentially, this should really be the job of the terminal emulator, at least for interactive tasks. Modern GNOME terminal emulators will indicate when you're running something as root, or in a container, by recoloring the appropriate parts of a window red / purple / whatever, and changing the terminal color scheme appropriately.

So I have seen the feature, and I really dislike the implementation of it, because it just keeps a list of command names it binds this too. That's just awfully hackish. I wish they'd come up with a proper ANSI OSC sequence instead so that we can tell them about this. But more importantly: this doesn't know the character cell where the priv change is placed, hence they tint the window title or something else that is "global", instead of telling me exactly in the output which part was privileged and which was not. I think this is really important to visualize actually, and they cannot do that, we however can.

I'd be happy to report such transitions to terminals via new OSC sequences, we can just make some new sequences up. But not sure there's interest in that, they seem to love hackish command name matches... Also, we'd need to find a way to detect this feature, i.e. some OSC sequence where we get a reply or so.

> The red dot is entirely redundant here, and actually counter-productive in some cases because this specific terminal emulator will actually show the icon of the container manager if it detects that you're inside of a container.

These are all hacks specific to the docker/podman ecosystem, hence wouldn't work for us.

> Right now we'd happily send a 1MB title to the terminal, which doesn't really make much sense

Ah well sure truncating so we don't send insane amounts of data into the terminal makes sense, of course. The terminal emulator layer probably does it for us, but I don't see any harm of doing it ourselves too.

As long as we're not truncating in the "visual" range of number of characters. It's perfectly feasible for the UI to show a couple hundred characters worth of title, and potentially more on an ultrawide monitor, so we should probably truncate at the ~2k char mark

> That's not actually true. We read the bg color from the terminal, and then shift it into a red hue. Maybe the algorithm for shifting the hue could be tweaked, but it's not true that we are "entirely unaware" of the color scheme. We are very much aware

Alright didn't know that, sorry about the misinformation then. In my testing, it seems that if my system is in dark mode I get the same shade of red no matter what the background color of the terminal is, giving my the false impression that run0 didn't take it into account. But switching into light mode does pick a different shade of red.

Of course, the terminal color scheme can also change at runtime, and in modern systems will do so relatively regularly depending on use-case. Here's what happens if I switch color schemes (which I do relatively often, i.e. if I take my laptop outside) while run0 is running:

![Screenshot from 2024-06-20 20-49-09](https://github.com/systemd/systemd/assets/11251606/e74b4d8f-b35f-443d-ad57-1e7ef08497ea)

![Screenshot from 2024-06-20 20-39-17](https://github.com/systemd/systemd/assets/11251606/ded30baa-8296-450c-af25-3848ede8cc5c)

So ulimately I don't think this is properly solvable from within a terminal client. We cannot control for nearly as many variables from within the limited API of the terminal as we could from the terminal emulator itself.

For instance: what if one of the numbered colors is red with the terminal's color scheme? Depending on the color scheme, it might end up being hard to read:

![Screenshot from 2024-06-20 20-47-33](https://github.com/systemd/systemd/assets/11251606/c336788a-d3ca-4f6f-8e38-7fff82564430)

> I  wish they'd come up with a proper ANSI OSC sequence instead so that we can tell them about this

Agreed.

Looks like Ptyxis, GNOME's state-of-the art containerized terminal app, already has some OSC codes in use for this. And `toolbx`, Fedora's podman wrapper, emits them. See: https://gitlab.gnome.org/chergert/ptyxis/#container-support

> this doesn't know the character cell where the priv change is placed

I'm really not sure about the limitations that terminals impose here. What's just not implemented versus what's impossible to implement.

CC @chergert for input on this specifically and the whole topic in general.

(Also, CC @allanday, @smwh because I think this is ultimately a design question)

> Also, we'd need to find a way to detect this feature, i.e. some OSC sequence where we get a reply or so.

Why? Seems more complicated than it's worth. Presumably the terminal app will either do something fancy with the information we give it, in which case great; or not, in which case oh well and maybe the user should just use the terminal app that does.

> they seem to love hackish command name matches
> [...]
> These are all hacks specific to the docker/podman ecosystem, hence wouldn't work for us

I presume that this has more to do with the current behavior of tools and less with them loving command name matching.

As mentioned above, in Ptyxis this isn't exclusive to docker/podman. There might not be an icon in the app for nspawn/systemd-run/etc, but that could be added quite easily. The actual end-goal mechanism here seems to be OSC sequences.

---

Also, unsure if this is a systemd bug or a terminal emulator bug. But run0 doesn't actually fill the whole line red:

![Screenshot from 2024-06-20 20-58-59](https://github.com/systemd/systemd/assets/11251606/3e492acf-ed1e-456f-83ab-20f7ab346b92)

UX-wise, I'm imagining something like https://www.warp.dev/. It highlights a block red if that command ultimately failed. We can do something similar for our rootful commands, and highlight the blocks different colors for containers, etc.

> Looks like Ptyxis, GNOME's state-of-the art containerized terminal app, already has some OSC codes in use for this. And `toolbx`, Fedora's podman wrapper, emits them. See: https://gitlab.gnome.org/chergert/ptyxis/#container-support

Are those OSC codes documented somewhere?

> Why? Seems more complicated than it's worth. Presumably the terminal app will either do something fancy with the information we give it, in which case great; or not, in which case oh well and maybe the user should just use the terminal app that does.

Well, not everyone runs Ptyxis. For example, I don't. I am happy to issue the OSC commands always. But if I need to suspect that they have no effect (like on my terminal here) I like a suitable fallback for this logic. Simply because I like if things work for myself.

> Also, unsure if this is a systemd bug or a terminal emulator bug. But run0 doesn't actually fill the whole line red:

hmm, the pytfwd code we have actually inserts an "erase-to-eol" sequence before each \n to ensure we erase things to the end line.

> Are those OSC codes documented somewhere?

They come from the Fedora patches in GNOME Terminal for the last 6-7 years.

However, we very much want to get away from them upstream in VTE and so GNOME 47 will introduce a concept called "termprops" which is a much better solution for PTY children to get/set variables coordinated with the terminal emulator. It will also serve as a better solution for notifications than what the Fedora patches do. 

The goal here is to patch podman/jhbuild/toolbox/distrobox/etc to emit these. Additionally, it will allow for bash/etc profiles to set a specific style scheme in the apps if they choose.

There is some effort to push the termprops up into the terminal working group on freedesktop, as the design is quite nice.

> Another thing that seems wrong is that all termprops are reset when the terminal is reset. What happens if you have an interactive shell running in a container, then run reset? It clears out all the termprops, and the terminal emulator forgets that it's in a container?

If you're looking for anything bulletproof and a PTY is involved, you'll probably be churning for the rest of your career.

But I will extremely caution about using anything related to the color palette and PTY in some automated fashion. Because in my experience, terminal color schemes are broken in so many flawed and unfixable ways other than "just pick one that works for your use case".

When I saw the run0 stuff doing colorization my first thought was "oh shit they don't know what they just bit off" if I'm to be a bit glib.
Also see #35845. While it is possible to suppress the implicit background changes there is currently no way to do the same if a background color is explicitly given as a flag.

review_comments: this can become static, if this is only checked from within ptyfwd.c
